query: The (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high-entropy alloy provides a large caloric response under applied-field and pressure-field operation but has poor integrity and tends to crack. Prior studies on related MM′X materials used epoxy-containing Mn0.98CoGe, obtaining compressive strengths of 152 and 218 MPa at two epoxy contents, and low-melting In composites, obtaining 48 MPa compressive strength and more than eight times the thermal conductivity of epoxy-containing samples under the reported conditions. These routes demonstrated gains in selected strength or heat-transport metrics, but the desired coexistence of robust integrity and high caloric performance remains unresolved. The target should also remain rare-earth-free. What single intervention could overcome this limitation without sacrificing caloric response? Present one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, quantitative or directional outcomes relative to the unchanged alloy, boundary conditions under applied-field, pressure, temperature, and loading regimes, supporting prior evidence, and a decisive controlled experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A controlled heat treatment that induces a fine, uniformly dispersed ductile secondary phase (via precipitation strengthening) in (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 will improve its mechanical integrity (i.e., reduce cracking under load) while preserving its high caloric response.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast (or conventionally processed) (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 high‐entropy alloy exhibiting a large caloric response but poor fracture toughness due to intrinsic brittleness.
generation.intervention: Apply an optimized heat-treatment protocol designed to trigger the in-situ formation of nanoscale, ductile precipitates without substantially altering the primary transformational phase responsible for the caloric effect. For example, hold the alloy at an intermediate temperature (e.g., 700–750 K) for a selected dwell time (around 1 hour) followed by a rapid quench.
generation.conditions: The treatment is performed in an inert atmosphere to prevent oxidation. Subsequent mechanical and caloric testing are conducted under applied magnetic or pressure fields at or near the alloy’s transition temperature (e.g., near room temperature) and under quasi-static compressive loading conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The formation and uniform dispersion of nanoscale ductile precipitates (secondary phase) at grain boundaries and within the microstructure.
generation.mechanism: The induced nanoscale precipitates act to impede crack initiation and propagation through conventional precipitation strengthening mechanisms. They enhance toughness without interfering significantly with the phase transformation behavior that provides the large caloric response, provided their volume fraction and distribution are optimized.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in compressive strength and fracture toughness (i.e., reduction in cracking) relative to the untreated alloy, with little to no degradation of the caloric effect magnitude.
generation.baseline: The untreated (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy, which while exhibiting a large caloric response, shows poor mechanical integrity and tendency to crack.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to be effective under applied-field (magnetic/pressure) operation near the caloric transition temperature and under quasi-static compressive loading; effects at extreme strain rates or in oxidizing environments are not addressed.
generation.uncertainty: There is uncertainty regarding the precise heat-treatment temperature/time parameters needed to optimize the precipitate size and distribution such that they reinforce the structure without interfering with the caloric phase transformation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of (MnNiSi)0.62(FeCoGe)0.38 alloy samples: one set undergoes the optimized heat treatment to induce precipitates (intervention group) while the other remains in the untreated state (control group). Conduct standardized compressive strength tests and measure caloric response (e.g., magnetocaloric or barocaloric effect) under identical applied-field and temperature conditions. Microstructural analysis using electron microscopy should confirm the presence and uniform distribution of precipitates in the intervention group.
measurements: Compressive strength and fracture toughness under quasi-static loading
Caloric response magnitude (e.g., adiabatic temperature change or isothermal entropy change) under applied fields
Microstructural characterization (grain and precipitate size, distribution, and volume fraction)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the heat-treated samples do not show a statistically significant improvement in mechanical integrity (i.e., no increase in compressive strength or toughness, with persistent cracking) or if the caloric response is substantially compromised (e.g., reduced by more than an acceptable margin relative to the baseline) compared to the untreated samples.
